Heading: the trailing 'a' is a footnote mark and is omitted. 'Curre, miser, curre; festina, duro tempus habes' is not a biblical text; 'duro' is read as 'dum' ('while you have time'). 'dilatus' is read as 'ditatus' ('enriched'); 'ah adventa' as 'ab adventu'. 'aliam gloriam sonumque habere velle dicunt' is obscure and may be corrupt; rendered literally. 'rerum collectione' ('of the gathered rewards') is uncertain.

Sermon II §3: the arithmetic is garbled as printed (366 days less 330 does not give 36; six days with their nights are 144 hours, not 150); the text seems corrupt or abbreviated here and is translated as it stands. §1: 'pelliceus ... pellis gratia' is an obscure etymology of the devil's name, rendered literally; 'defectatur' read as 'delectatur'. Sermon II breaks off after §3 in this edition. Stray footnote marks ('abstinentiam a', 'abstinuit a') omitted.

Scanning errors read as evident: passuros > passurus, cautibus > cantibus, redo > recto, 70X > vox, prasenti > praesenti, concutieutem > concutientem, nostra > nostrae, veleris > veteris, m caeleris > in caeteris, sabhato > sabbato, fraudo > fraude, cis > eis, cos > eos. 'Pascha petitum' is probably for 'Pascha petentium' (Pascha of the petitioners); *competentes* are candidates for baptism. 'plebs Hebraeorum Dominum praecedentium et sequentium' is grammatically awkward; rendered as 'those going before the Lord and those following'. 'si ... senserimus' (sermon III) is obscure; rendered 'if we shall be made to feel'.

Several scanning errors read as evident: 'fuero' as 'fuere' (they happened); 'mula' as 'multa' (many idols); 'qu a' as 'quia'; 'ter beatissimi' taken as 'fratres beatissimi' (most blessed brothers); 'munificare' as 'mortificare' (mortify).

nodes.text: 1. Since today's reading has called us to the race of the spiritual stadium, dearly beloved brothers, we ought to consider with a most attentive mind how we must run and what we must abstain from. Literally, the stadium is said to be the fourth part of a mile, which Hercules is said to have been the first to run in a single breath. In ancient times a post was set up at its end, with a crown woven of flowers placed on top, and there a band of unencumbered young men used to run to win it, so that one of them, the first, if he could, by running faster, might seize the prize, which we call a crown, and through this would have the praise of the king and the onlookers, and then many gifts in particular. Many strove for this with a common purpose, but all were beaten by one, who, because he was faster in the race, seemed more worthy than the rest of the gathered rewards. And as much as the victor rejoiced, enriched with royal gifts, so much did the vanquished grieve, not only deprived of the gifts but also disgraced by the shame of their slowness. They did indeed abstain from foods that harm running, but not equally, for his abstinence had been the greater who was faster than the rest in the race. Do not be surprised, brothers, that the apostle gave an example to imitate, drawn from pagan superstition, for the protection of souls, so that any of you might think that the practices of the gentiles are in nothing to be followed, from whom the Christian religion, at Christ's urging, has made us strangers. Let your charity know first, then, that the church has taken over for itself certain holy things from their rite, which are to be followed not carnally but spiritually; and of these is this example, most useful, which today's reading has set before us. For the end of the stadium, which was measured out to them for running, signifies the end of the present life, which has been given to us for the race of our salvation, as the Lord says and warns: "Run, wretch, run; hurry while you have time, lest you fall into death." For they ran to win a temporal and corruptible prize, to receive earthly gifts from a mortal king; let us run better, to win a spiritual and incorruptible prize after the end of the flesh, so that from the King of kings, who is eternal and immortal, we may receive eternal and unfailing gifts, hearing his longed-for voice saying: "Come, you who labour," etc. They abstained from rich foods so as to be made more unencumbered in the race; let us abstain better, not so much from foods as from vices, so that we may be swift to run. But that out of a great throng of young men one won the prize while the rest ran in vain, this, as far as it concerns us, dearest brothers, is much to be feared: namely, lest all of us who have resolved to run for the crown be beaten by one. Hence the Apostle warns: "So run that you may obtain." And how shall we be able to obtain it, since we do not want to run; and if at some time we begin to run, alas, worn out by the grossness of our vices, we shamefully give out in the race! For although the whole church is divided into the clerical and lay orders, there is no one among them who runs for the crown of glory; but some, anxious with insatiable greed, some, polluted with unbridled pleasure, some, swollen with the pride of worldly pomp, not only do not want to run, but do not even know how to open their eyes to win the crown. Hence the Psalmist: "All have turned aside together; they have become useless." And the Prophet: "As the people, so the priest." For we are so blinded and thrust down into a kind of pit of forgetfulness that, thinking nothing of the future, we suppose there is no other life besides this one, in which we pursue our pleasures. And to say more, many, raving, while they feed their greedy minds on voluptuous desires and rage like wolves against those subject to them, say that they wish to have another glory and renown. Such people lose the nature of man and take on the nature of four-footed beasts, which irrationally and shamelessly are ever bent on belly and lust. For the Creator of things set man over earthly creatures in such a way that, using temporal things well, he might after death enjoy eternal ones. What must be done about this, dearest brothers? For we are all lost unless we are soon raised up by divine mercy. For it calls us to run, saying: "Walk, lest the darkness overtake you." At its call, if we will take up the race again, it will be granted not to one only but to very many to attain the crown. And just as [the same man] did not win in every race, but one who had just been beaten would, with renewed strength, become the victor, so let us, if we have been beaten until now, take care to be victors from now on. For the way of running is set before our eyes, and the slower we have been on it, the faster we can be, if we will.

2. For how can we, sluggish and lazy, cease from the race, when we have as our admonisher not only the apostle, for the crown, but also our Saviour himself, for receiving the denarius? For he, the supreme householder, who planted the vineyard, that is, the holy church, promises to give the denarius of heavenly reward to us who entered the vineyard to labour late, that is, at the end of the world, likening us to the first labourers, who from morning until evening bore the burden of the day and the heat. For you heard him, in the true and fitting parable set forth in the gospel, inviting workers to the cultivation of his vineyard in the morning, at the third, sixth, ninth and eleventh hour, and paying an equal denarius to all when the work was done. And if you desire the meanings of the hours you have heard, learn that the morning was from Adam to Noah; the third hour from Noah to Abraham; the sixth from Abraham to Moses; the ninth from Moses to the coming of our Lord and Saviour; the eleventh was from the coming of the Lord to the end of the world, in which we, the last workers, have entered the vineyard. But because we are idle and slow in the work, we cannot be certain of the denarius. Let us therefore strive to work faster, so that we may be secure of the denarius; and since today we are called by the supreme householder, let us not despise his call, but strive to enter the vineyard to labour. For he instituted the present fast for this purpose, that the innumerable sins we have committed through delight of the flesh on the other days of the year we may strive to wipe away at this time through penance and mortification of the flesh.

3. Moreover, this day, which is as it were the gateway of the fasts and takes from us the song of gladness, that is, the alleluia, expresses through the whole course of its office the voice of a penitent lamenting, teaching us that we ought to cease from immoderate gladness and remain in the weeping and tears of penance. So this night, repeating its name many times, we addressed the alleluia itself, desiring in a way to keep it back like a guest, saying to it: "Stay with us today," and the rest. We also bade it a last farewell, saying: "May a good angel go with you, so that you may return to us again with joy," so that we may know that we shall not rejoice perfectly before, renewed by the body and blood of our Redeemer, we receive that song back with rejoicing. The antiphon of the mass, commonly called the introit, laments with the penitents, saying: "The sorrows of death have surrounded me, and in my tribulation." The collect, with the response, sounds the affliction of penance. Then that chant which we have put in place of the alleluia (which is called the tract because it has long chants) teaches penitents to cry to God with deep groaning. And so the other words of the office, arranged in order, seem to express not the gladness of those rejoicing but the grief and sorrow of sinners.

4. As to the name of the day, which is called Septuagesima, if you ask, know that it took its name not from the number of days, as those suppose who reckon so many days from it to the Easter feast, but from the perfection of the number, from which that number took its beginning. Now this number consists of ten multiplied seven times: of these the seven pertains to the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the ten to the ten commandments of the law; which are so joined to each other that neither the gifts of the Holy Spirit without the commandment of the law, nor the commandments of the law without the gift of the Holy Spirit, can be kept by anyone; and whoever keeps the one will without doubt have the other. This number rightly suits penitents, so that the grace of the Holy Spirit which they lost by sinning they may be able to recover by keeping the ten commandments of the law, especially at this time. Otherwise, according to some, it is called Septuagesima literally because the people of Israel were held captive in Babylon for that many years, and returning from there after a long time, consecrated a fast to God of the same number in commemoration of that deliverance. But since it suits penitents both according to history and according to allegory, let us strive at this time to weep for our sins, so that our souls after this life, which turns in seven days, delivered from Babylon, that is, from the captivity of hell, and enriched with the gifts of the Holy Spirit, may joyfully receive from the King of kings both the unfading crown for the race and the denarius for the day's labour in the vineyard. Amen.

1. Strive, dearest ones, you who desire to cleanse your souls from sin, that you do not draw back from this way of fasting and amendment which you have undertaken to keep, by any byway of foulness. For through the deceptions of the ancient enemy a certain custom has been imposed on some of you on this day, not so much to be followed as to be despised: that because of the meat of the flesh alone, which is not taken from us today, you think you may do every delight of the body and every foul thing freely, having found this pretext in yourselves, that because it is lawful for you to eat meat, it is lawful also to indulge the pleasures of the flesh. These are not the works of Christians but of pagans. For the pagans, who are also called gentiles, celebrating the festival of their gods, that is, of Jupiter, Saturn, Minerva and Venus, after immense gluttony of food and drink and foul revels, used to gather outside the city at the theatre, which is also called a brothel; and there they wearied their bodies in debauchery, first with jests of various kinds, and at last with the harlots who lay hidden in the recesses of that same theatre. To this filthy foulness, as Paulus Orosius relates, the very devil whom they worshipped provoked them, so that to him to whom they paid sacrifice from the victims of animals they might pay sacrifice also from the strength of their own bodies. For the devil is polluted and unclean, and requires a polluted and unclean sacrifice for himself: hence he is called *pelliceus*, which is interpreted 'for the sake of the skin', because he delights greatly in lust, which is roused by the beauty of the skin. But as great as the distance is between the service of God and of the devil, so great is it between the life of those who are called Christians from Christ, and of those who, subject to the devil, serve him in all things. For this reason, brothers, we must cease from this and from every evil custom on the present day, since this day is the head not only of the fasts but also of the ages. It is therefore to be venerated with great worship and devotion, and not polluted with lustful pleasures, because in name and mystery it appears to be consecrated above the others. It is called by the Lord the Lord's day, because he placed it first in the order of days, and because, having overcome death, which he took on for us unworthy ones, and having conquered the enemy, from whose power he snatched us, he rose mightily from the dead on it, and appointed it for us to keep in honour of his resurrection. How then do we desire to rise from the death of the soul, if we will not honour the day of the Lord's resurrection? And on what reasoning do we think to purify our minds through fasts, if we wish to enter polluted through the gate of the fasts?

2. Perhaps, as I rebuke such things and reprove my own sins together with the iniquities of others, some unbridled person, obeying the pleasures of the body more than the laws of God, will answer me: "You, who preach that the natural union of male and female and the bond of love established from the beginning should be put asunder, ask what is altogether impossible and useless, that during some fast I should abstain from the woman, who is my flesh, as from foods." To him I, although a sinner, shall answer with an easy word: God did not give the goods of the world for us to abuse them, but for us to use them justly. For marriage, like the other riches of the world, is good while it is held justly; when unjustly, it is turned into sin. Hence Gregory: whatever we receive for the use of life, we turn to the use of vices. Nor do I preach the separation of so sacred a partnership, but I enjoin abstinence for the short time of thirty-six days. For what does it profit to abstain from meats and not lay aside the works of the flesh? You who have lived the whole year given over to these and other delights ought at least to cease for God in this small space. Why are you called a man (*vir*) from the strength (*virtus*) of the body, if you do not have this strength in your mind, so that for God, who gave you all things and from whom you daily ask for greater, you cannot fast for a tenth part of the year?

3. For whoever looks closely will find no more than thirty-six days, which are the tithe of the year, in this same abstinence. For since the whole year consists of 366 days, if 330 are subtracted, they consecrate to fasting as many days as I have said. Of these six days, then, which together with their nights consist of 150 hours, the tenth part is fifteen hours. But because from these we cannot gather a whole day with the following night, which we might add to the aforesaid number and devote to fasting, ecclesiastical custom has decreed that what is not rendered in that [day] be made up on the Sundays of the same season by fasting from meat and from carnal pleasures. For on these, because they are consecrated in the very name of God, the refreshment of food is granted and the licence to sin is taken away. What brings life and is better is given to us; what brings death and is worse is taken from us. And if we do not pollute these [days] with vices and carnal defilement, we certainly restore with them the full tithes of the whole year. But since to us, reborn in the sacred font and tasting the flesh no longer of the figurative but of the true lamb, it was said by the Lord himself: "Unless your righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven," the Christian religion has decreed that not only these thirty-six on account of the tithe of the year, but with them also the four which begin from the head of the fast, on account of the perfection of so great a mystery, should be changed into forty days of fasting. For this Lenten fast has great authority from the Law, from the Prophets and from the Gospel. For Moses the lawgiver fasted forty days that he might receive the law. Likewise Elijah, the greatest of the prophets, who was found worthy to be caught up into heaven in a fiery chariot, when he was persecuted by Jezebel, first fed with angelic food, afterwards abstained from all food for as many [days].

1. Now that the season of Lent is passing and the joys of the most holy Resurrection are drawing near, dearly beloved brothers, the commemoration of the Lord's passion comes to us yearly, which today strikes the universal Church with a tearful recital. And although many days remain from this one until that which was found worthy to see its maker crucified in particular, nevertheless the holy fathers have committed this same passion to us to be recited through the days that follow, above all blessed Gregory, who in all the church offices, day and night, from here until the Paschal feast, brings in the words and the mourning of the passion, suggesting that we ought to weep for him without whom we can have no joy perfectly. Whoever of us, then, trust that we are members of our Redeemer, let us feel the pain and injury of so great a head. Hence the prophet: "The whole head is sick and the whole heart grieving; from the sole of the foot to the crown there is no soundness in it." And the Apostle: "If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it." Since we know that the higher and more honourable member, namely Christ, who is our head and crown, suffered, let us, the lower members, suffer with him: above all since he willed to suffer not for any fault he had committed, but for our redemption, that he might redeem us from the ancient servitude of the devil and make us perpetual inhabitants of the heavenly homeland, from which we were shut out as captives. For he, ineffably merciful, willed to cleanse our sins and our ancient iniquities not with gold or any kind of metal, nor with cloaks of beautiful variety, nor even with the victims of other animals, but with his own body sacrificed to God the Father on the altar of the cross, and with his most precious blood poured out. Hence the prophet: "Truly he bore our pains, he carried our infirmities." And our mediator himself said to the Father: "Burnt offering and [offering] for sin you did not demand; then I said, behold, I come." And the sense is: "O God the Father, since I saw that you did not seek a burnt offering of animals for the redemption of the human race, I said at once: behold, I come to be sacrificed for the salvation of my people." See, dearest brothers, we have heard that Christ was sacrificed for us: from which we can both greatly rejoice and be sad: rejoice, because happy the fault which had such and so great a Redeemer; be sad, because we see no imitator of so great a passion. For he, having died bodily, requires as sacrifice not only the death of our body, if need be, but the amendment of life and the humbling of the spirit. That is, that our spirit, marvelling at so great and ineffable humility of its maker, should tremble, and overcoming the allurements of the flesh, should have a kind of compassion with him who suffered. Hence it is [said]: "A troubled spirit is a sacrifice to God." And although it is impossible for our bodily frailty to follow his immense deity, yet we follow him well according to the measure of our humanity if we slay the vices of the body through fasting, prayers and vigils, if we rejoice to remain clean and shining before his eyes. Hence the prophet: "Wash yourselves, be clean," and the rest.

2. But how, when the fury of a persecutor threatens, are we going to lay down our life for him, we who for love of him cannot fast even for a short time from vices and from foods of any kind? In what, then, do we imitate his passion, we who restrain our bodies from no filthiness? For besides this, what is worse, we resist his commands strongly and are opposed to him as to an enemy. For while he cries out in the Old Testament, "You shall not kill, you shall not steal," and the other commands of the law, we, as if provoking his anger against us, insane and out of our minds, both commit adultery and kill and steal; moreover, the more all vices are forbidden us, the more we take care to pursue and love them. Likewise, while he threatens in the New Testament of the Gospel, "Everyone who says to his brother 'raca', and who says 'fool', shall be liable to the fire of Gehenna," we on the contrary, touched by the zeal of envy, proudly and stubbornly heap every insult and reproach upon our brothers. Therefore we ought to restrain our mind from such things and from things like them, if we hope to be partakers of his redemption. For he is the true priest and high priest of the good things to come, who offered to God his Father not the blood of goats and bulls but himself, namely the spotless lamb, cleansing our conscience from dead works, that is, from sins; and through this he entered once into the holy place, that he may now appear before the face of God the Father for us. For the other priests, having slaughtered the flesh of animals according to the custom of the old law, entered once each year into the holy place; this priest for ever, who came not to abolish the law but to fulfil it, not each year but in the last year of his life, having sacrificed himself on the altar of the cross, entered once into the holy place, that is, into heaven, so that he might unlock to the servants who follow him through faith the secrets of the Father, which after the end he will grant them to possess. The other priests, when the time of sacrifice was completed, took care to return to their own homes, to come back to the temple the following year; he, having accomplished the mystery of his passion and resurrection, returned to his own palace of heaven, to come not the following year but at the end of the world, to examine the merits of the good and the wicked with just scrutiny and to render rewards to the good and punishments to the wicked. What shall we do on that day, brothers, on which we shall have to give account not only for evil works but also for idle words? And if we shall be made to feel all the faults of the tongue, which we count as nothing, what is to be feared concerning the other members, namely the hands and feet and the rest, which we know without doubt have done many unlawful things? For if we pay the penalty for all the faults we have committed, we are eternally damned and lost. Therefore let each of us, as much as he loves his own soul, so much blot out his past sins through penance, and beware lest he repeat them, and let him not kindle again what he has once extinguished by the grace of God. For he who repeats a sin over which he has already groaned provokes God to anger against himself, so that when called upon he does not hear him. Hence he says through Solomon: "I called, and you refused; you despised all my counsel and neglected my rebukes: I also will laugh at your destruction, and mock when what you feared has come upon you." How dreadful is the voice, dearly beloved brothers, by which our Redeemer threatens that he will laugh at our destruction! Wherefore let us constantly open the ears of our mind to his commands, so that in the judgement we may see him not terrible but gentle. And how shall we be able to endure him terrible and angry against us, we who in the present life can scarcely bear his lightning or his thunder for fear? And if we are terrified for a time by the movement of a single creature, with what fortitude shall we be able to await the Creator coming with fire to judge, and shaking not only the earth but also the heavens? For as the Psalmist says: "Fire shall burn in his sight, and around him a mighty tempest." And the judge himself says through the prophet: "Yet once more, and I will move not only the earth but also heaven." Fear greatly, brothers, the coming of that judge, in whose fixed judgement there will be no room for redemption. Cease from depraved morals and from the evil habit of a shameful life, and be eager to suffer with your Redeemer, so that with him you may both rise again from the tombs of vices and after the judgement happily ascend to the heavenly kingdom. Amen.

1. Gladdened by the delight of the present day, dearest brothers, you ought to recognise attentively the mysteries with which it shines, so that the instructed mind may examine inwardly where the joys of gladness that we celebrate outwardly arise from. But lest a superfluity of words breed weariness in your minds, especially since the office of this day is drawn out in very long chants and most pleasing jubilations to our God, I shall first try to give you a brief foretaste concerning its name, which is distinguished by various terms. For it is called the day of Palms, or of Flowers, and of Branches, and also Hosanna, Pascha of the petitioners or of the *competentes*, and [the day] of those washing heads. And although these are so named in popular usage, yet all retain a definite and fitting meaning. It is called the day of Palms because on it our Lord, seated on a little ass, went on to Jerusalem to suffer for the salvation of the human race; and a very great crowd of rejoicing people met him with branches of palms and of various trees, crying: "Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord." It is also called the day of Flowers because holy mother Church, in commemoration of so great a joy, has willed on this day above the others in the yearly cycle to carry blessed and consecrated flowers while singing, so that she may rejoicing go to meet her Redeemer. It is also called the day of Branches because for the same reason not only palms but also green branches are carried today by the sons of the Church. It is called Hosanna because the Hebrew people, those going before the Lord and those following, were seen to sing to that same Lord "Hosanna", which is translated in Latin "Save". It is called Pascha of the petitioners or of the *competentes* because on this day the creed, that is, the belief of the holy faith, used to be handed over to the *competentes*, the neophytes, so that those who were hastening to receive the grace of God at the Paschal solemnity might know the faith which they would have to confess. For they are called *competentes* as if "petitioning together", that is, petitioning for the grace of God. The common people call this day [that] of those washing heads, because on that day it was the custom to wash the heads of the infants who were to be anointed on Holy Saturday, lest perhaps, soiled by the observance of Lent, they should come to the anointing. This week is called greater either because a greater sobriety is kept in it, or because a greater office is celebrated in it than in the other weeks.

2. Let these things briefly said about the names of this day suffice: some of them, as they are understood literally, so they remain; others signify something else allegorically. For in all the Scripture of the Old and New Testament the palm has always signified victory. By the palm branches, then, is designated that victory by which our Lord through his death destroyed our death, and through the trophy of the cross overcame the devil, the prince of death. By the flowers is expressed the fragrance of virtue, captivated by which faithful souls accompany their king as he goes to Jerusalem, that is, to holy Church, so that, celebrating the Pasch with him, that is, the passing over, they may deserve to rise with him to heavenly things. By the branches of trees are signified the sayings of the ancient prophets, which he gathers and strews on the way who instructs by examples the simple and less learned hearts of the brothers, lest they wander from the way of truth. And that hosanna, so often repeated and redoubled by the people, signifies the unity of our faith in which we ought to live; for although there is among the faithful people a diversity of rank as well as of sex and age, yet with one mouth and one praise of confession we ought to cry out to our Saviour, saying: Hosanna, that is, save, or make safe; for it is a Hebrew word which, expressed in Latin, means "save", or "make safe your people", or "the whole world".

3. But since such names are fitted to this day from the fitting meanings of the mysteries, it must be shown to you, dearest ones, in some brief account, by what works of our Saviour it is made illustrious. For as the holy evangelist relates, six days before the old Pasch, which are counted from yesterday, Jesus came to Bethany, to the house of Simon the leper, where he had raised Lazarus, and they made him a supper there; where also Mary, taking a pound of ointment, anointed the feet of the Lord and wiped them with her hair; and when Judas the traitor was indignant at this, Jesus answered in praise of the woman: "She has done a good work for me," and the rest that follows on this matter in the Passion. Following the custom of this good work, the holy man Gregory on this very day, namely yesterday, occupied himself entirely with giving alms and washing the feet of the poor, so that what the most devout woman did to the head, that is, to Christ, he might do to his members, that is, to the poor. Hence that same day, remaining without an office of its own, is headed thus in the Sacramentary: "On Saturday there is no public station, when the lord pope gives alms." If you wish to pluck an allegorical flower from this deed, know that the ointment signifies righteousness, and therefore it is said to have been a pound. For he who perfectly keeps righteousness without doubt washes the feet of the Lord; and he who by living well loves mercy anoints his feet with ointment. And he who gives abundantly to the poor wipes the Lord's feet with his hair. The house, then, was filled with the fragrance of the ointment, that is, the whole world, both by the fame of so very devout a woman and by the virtue of the faithful who imitate her in such things. For the fact that the Son of God, about to suffer, went to Bethany six days before the Pasch signifies that the man, created on the sixth day, whom the serpent's deceit had destroyed, he was hastening, passing through Bethany, that is, through the house of obedience, to redeem with his own blood on that same sixth day. Going out from the aforesaid town of Bethany on the following day, namely the fifth day before the Pasch, which is today, he sent two of his disciples to Jerusalem, saying to them: "Go into the village which is opposite you, and you will find an ass and a colt: untie them and bring them to me." Untying them, they brought them to Jesus and put their garments on them, and made him sit on top. When the crowd that had come for the feast day heard that Jesus was going to Jerusalem, they took palm branches and came out to meet him, and cried: "Hosanna, blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord."

4. But since these deeds of the Lord, recorded in the words of the evangelist, are clear enough according to the letter, for they happened just as they sound, the mystical sense must be laid open by us, briefly, for it is hidden from all but the wise. For the two disciples signify the two orders of preachers, one among the circumcision, the other among the gentiles; or [they signify] Peter and Philip, whom Christ sent to Jerusalem, that is, to holy Church. One of them, Philip, led Samaria, as the ass, to the faith of Christ; the other, Peter, led Cornelius from the gentiles, as the colt. Again, by the two animals two peoples are figured, namely the Jewish and the gentile. These were tied up when the disciples came, because each people was bound by the chains of its sins. The garments of the apostles are either the teachings of the virtues or the works of righteousness. Hence the psalmist: "Let your priests be clothed with righteousness." And the very large crowd which strewed its garments on the way signifies the countless multitude of martyrs, who, stripping themselves of their own clothing, make a way for the simpler, by which they may be able to come to the vision of peace. For by the little ass on which he sat are figured the simple hearts of the gentiles, which remained as if untamed, bound by no reins of discipline, going to many idols as it was led; and the Lord, presiding over it and guiding it, led it to the vision of eternal peace. Finally, it is believed to have been done not without the reason of a great mystery that the Lord, going to Jerusalem specially on this day, made use of the service of beasts of burden, and wished various adornments of palms and branches or flowers to be carried around him, and himself to be called king and Lord: all of which he had often refused to have done before when coming to Jerusalem. For he entered with such glory for this reason: that, since he knew the time of his passion was already at hand, he might force the minds of the Jews to be roused against him, so that through the death of his body he might destroy the death of our souls. Therefore, most blessed brothers, we who recall his passion, even if we cannot all die for him, and, the slanderers of the Church having been pacified, have no war with them, let us nevertheless take care to mortify the vices of our members, so that after the mourning of the passion, receiving the joys of the resurrection, we may be able to rise with him from vices to the height of the virtues. Amen.
